messages.body_plain:
Hi Ruth.  Good question -- this appears to be a bug (thanks for the  
catch!).  The na.omit arguments of '[.network' and 'is.adjacent' (at  
least) need fixing.

The good news is that the missing data structure is not lost:  The  
easiest way to see it is to type
net3p$gal$design,
which is itself a network object giving the positions of the original  
NAs.

Thus, a simple hack to work around this (until it can be fixed for  
real!) is:

"[.network"<-function(x,...,na.omit=TRUE) {
   oldf <- get("[.network", pos=match("package:network",search()))
   out <- oldf(x,...)
   if (!na.omit) {
     out[oldf(x$gal$design,...)==1] <- NA
   }
   out
}


and this seems to work at least on simple examples, e.g.:
 > m <- matrix(0,3,3)
 > m[1,2] <- NA
 > network(m)[1:2,2:3,na.omit=FALSE]
    2 3
1 NA 0
2  0 0


Hope this helps.

Dave

messages.body_plain:
In brief, I have 4 nets stored as an edgelist with a group of attribute variables.  I can't get the edge attributes into my network object.

I realize you all have answered questions similar to this before, such as at:
    [statnet_help] importing edgelist with multiple attributes  on  Sun Mar 11 20:45:50 PDT 2007

But I can't get it to work for my particular data configuration.  Please, help!


DATA STRUCTURE

I have four networks over a large set of nodes (~3300).  They are stored in a data.frame as:

  SENDING RECEIVE cvs   rsurg  ccu   micu
1  260094  260040       0        0       0        1
2  310063  310002       0        0       0        1
3  370047  370028       8        0       1        0
4  390192  390119       0        4       0        1
5  410008  410007       0        0       1        0
6  510012  510007       2        0       1        0
7   80007  210019       0        0       1        0
 ...

where SENDING and RECEIVE are the arbitrary ID's of the nodes.  (They are numeric, but are not sequential; using as.character for the network call has worked well.)

CVS, SURG, CCU and MICU are, respectively, the value of the directed edges between the two nodes.

Two nodes may be connected reciprocally, but need not be.  All node pairs in the data have at least 1 directed edge in 1 of the nets, but may have a directed edge in all 4 nets.  This is a sparse network, so most node pairs do not occur at all.  A given edge pair appears on only one line in the data.

I would like to create a set of 4 graphs over the same node set.  I cannot figure out how to use set.edge.value to create 4 attributes for each edge, one for each network.

FAILED CODE:
# This creates the network appropriately, but attaches the edge values to the wrong edges;
attach(jan29.core.recast)
core_net<-network( array(
   c(as.character(SENDING), as.character(RECEIVE)),
   dim=c(length(SENDING),2)),
   directed=TRUE, hyper=FALSE, loops=FALSE, multiple=FALSE)
set.edge.value(core_net,"cvs",jan29.core.recast$cvs);

I am guessing that the process of creating the network reorders the edgelist in some way to create the internal network edgelist, so that my data.frame edgelist and the internal network object edgelist are no longer synchronized.   But I don't know how to fix it.  I would appreciate any help.

best,
  Jack

Hi all,

 

I have a 79x79 directed network of email traffic that I'm trying to fit to
an ERGM model. I've run into some problems with the gwdsp (geometrically
weighted dyadwise shared partner) and gwodegree (geometrically weighted
out-degree) parameters.

 

If I include gwdsp in the model, it just does not run and gives the
following output:

> email25.e_gwd0<-ergm(email25.net~edges+gwdsp(0,fixed=TRUE),verbose=TRUE)

Evaluating network in model

Initializing model.

Initializing Metropolis-Hastings proposal.

Fitting initial model.

Fitting ERGM.

Iteration 1 of at most 3 with parameter: 

        edges gwdsp.fixed.0 

    -2.620430      0.000000 

Error in ergm.mcmcslave(Clist, MHproposal, eta0, MCMCparams, maxedges,  : 

  NA/NaN/Inf in foreign function call (arg 15)

 

If I include gwodegree in the model, it runs but some strange things happen.
First, the model becomes degenerate, even though the model is ok with
gwidegree. If I include gwodegree with gwidegree or with gwesp, TNT sampler
stops accepting all proposals, and thus the model is degenerate. Also, When
fixed=TRUE at 0, gwidegree parameter is named gwidegree.fixed.0, however,
gwodegree is only named gwodegree, suggesting that it may not actually be
fixed. 

 

Any ideas/fixes would be greatly appreciated. Thanks!

 

Jichao Qian

example) MPI-enabled Ruby or Python interpreters (the latter using pypar 
and RPy).

Simon

   Total       46    29       13    88

So let's focus on the (outcasts, loyal) and (loyal, outcasts) pairs  
since there are only a few of them.  Here they are:

 > g = samplike %v% "group"
 > e = as.matrix.network.edgelist(samplike)
 > f = function(row,g) any(g[row]=="outcasts") && any(g[row]=="loyal")
 > e[apply(e,1,f,g),]
      [,1] [,2]
[1,]   15    2
[2,]    1   15
[3,]    2   15

In other words, (15,2) is counted as the one example of a (from =  
outcasts, to = loyal) tie, whereas (1,15) and (2,15) are the two  
(loyal, outcasts) ties.

Now for the output of the nodeifactor and nodeofactor:

nodeofactor.group.loyal

13                         34

output tells me that there are 29 (=5+23+1) ties to loyal nodes.  I  
can also verify this directly:

[1] 29

So I'm wondering:  First, do you get the same output that I did in  
this example?  Second, would you have EXPECTED to see this output for  
this example, or do you, say, interpret terms like "From" and "to"  
and "in" and "out" differently?

Hope this helps.  I'll be curious to hear what you find.

Dave

messages.body_plain:
Carter and Simon,

Thanks for your notes.  Simon's experience is certainly a dispiriting  
tale in terms of trying to do this on my own, although I may be stupid  
enough to try.  (I'll let the list know if I succeed at all.)

I guess my thoughts are:
  - Permutation methods in social network are widespread
  - "limitations on computational feasibility" were invoked rampantly  
at the last INSNA
  - you can't buy an Apple desktop machine with less than 8 cores  
right now; does Intel even make single-core chips any longer?

Given all this, I would strongly support any development work that can  
be done.  I suspect there may be induce-able demand -- until people  
appreciate the performance advantages of effective parallelization,  
they don't ask for it.  At the same time, not having well-parallelized  
software, there is no reason to make the modest marginal investment in  
multi-core machines.

I would certainly volunteer to be a beta-site; I'm just not good  
enough at writing code to really meaningfully contribute.  Please let  
me know what else I can do to help.

best,
   Jack


For other intrepid souls, I'll add a few other references I found:
- UWashington (home of statnet?) apparently developed SNOW: http://www.bepress.com/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1016&context=uwbiostat
- some gene selection work has been done and parallelized in R: http://www.pubmedcentral.nih.gov/articlerender.fcgi?artid=2034606

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jenine,

Because your model contains only "dyadic-independence" terms, 
interpretation is relatively straightforward. I will outline it below, but 
you should definitely turn to the Social Networks special issue (Vol 29, 
issue 2) or the JoSS special issue (currently available as the "Online 
Users Guide" at statnetproject.org) for more background.

The ERGM model is a logit model, so that coefficients are interpretable as 
additions to the logodds.  The ERGM model can be interpreted either in 
terms of the probability of a given edge or arc existing, or in terms of 
the probability of an entire network being observed; let's use the former, 
since it's generally more intuitive.

In this framework, to get the logodds of a given edge/arc (given the rest 
of the network), you multiply each "change statistic" by its corresponding 
coefficient, and then add these terms together.  A "change statistic" is 
the amount by which any of the statistics in your model changes when you 
add the new edge/arc.

So, for instance, your model is:

> y ~ edges + nodefactor(grade) + nodefactor(age group) + nodematch(gender)

If I make up coefficient values of

edges =	-5.1
nodefactor.grade08 = 0.3
nodefactor.grade09 = 0.2
nodefactor.agegroup01 = 0.4
nodefactor.agegroup02 = 0.8
nodematch.gender = 2.1

Then, the logodds of an edge or arc (in either direction) between a 
male/grade8/agegroup1 and a female/grade8/agegroup2 would be:

-5.1(1) + 0.3(2) + 0.4(1) 0.8(1) = -3.3

since by forming this edge/arc, the total number of edges/arcs increases 
by 1, the total degree for all grade 8 actors increases by 2, the total 
degree for age group 1 actors increases by 1, and the total degree for all 
age group 2 actors increases by 1.

If the same two actors had been of the same sex instead of different 
sexes, then the logodds would increase by 2.1 (since the number of 
same-sex edges would increase by 1), bringing the logodds to -1.2.

The probabilities corresponding to logodds of -3.3 and -1.2 are .036 and 
.23, respectively.

If you have a dyadic dependence model (i.e. with terms like triangle or 
degree), then interpretation gets slightly more complex, because you need 
to know about the other edges/arcs in the network to know how likely a 
given edge/arc is.

I hope this helps.

Cheers,
Steve
